KEY MESSAGE 1...

Showers and thunderstorms entering, and forming in, the middle 
Ohio Valley early this morning, were tied to a mid/upper-level 
short wave trough, which exits this afternoon. Thunderstorms 
this morning will continue to have the potential for heavy 
downpours given precipitable water values peaking in the 2-2.25 
inch range, as well as strong wind gusts within the heavy 
downbursts, and pockets of modest shear through 8 km associated 
with the short wave.

The Weather Prediction Center continues their Marginal Risk for
Excessive Rainfall for southwestern portions of the forecast 
area Tuesday for today where the lead outflow boundary and 
trailing boundary laid down by a weakening convective complex 
can focus the heaviest and most numerous cells this morning.
They have also added a Marginal Risk area in northeast WV, the
tail end of a larger area over the northeastern U.S. with the 
exiting short wave trough.

The Weather Prediction Center has also issued a Mesoscale
Precipitation Discussion for southern portions of the forecast 
area through early this morning, citing the well-defined mid-
level vort center advancing eastward across the lower Ohio 
Valley as evident on GOES-R imagery, and moisture and 
instability transport fed by the 40 kt nocturnal low level jet 
as evident on RLX VAD wind profile.

Showers and thunderstorms end, or at least decreases in
coverage, from west to east this afternoon as the system exits.
However, as the clouds scatter out this afternoon, heating could
allow additional thunderstorms to pop up. Coverage is expected 
to be scattered at most, but any storms that do pop up can 
produce stronger wind gusts, and the Storm Prediction Center 
keeps the northeast half of the forecast area within the 
southern extent of a Marginal Severe Thunderstorm Risk area, for
a damaging wind threat. This is where CAPE, and shear through 8
km, are forecast to be higher, and where CAMs suggest 
development. 

A mid/upper-level ridge crosses Wednesday night through 
Thursday night, but with embedded flat waves, most notably 
Thursday afternoon. Models continue to advertise high CAPE, 3-4
KJ/kg, Thursday afternoon, amid a very warm and moist 
environment that features h85 temperatures near 20 C, h850 
theta e values as high as 350 K, PW values of around 1.75 
inches and surface dew points potentially in the low to mid 70s.

While shear will be weak, the juicy, very unstable air couple
with the flat wave could support robust storms capable of heavy
rainfall which could lead to locally strong to severe
microbursts, as well as high rainfall rates.

The Storm Prediction Center has upgraded the Marginal Risk for 
Severe Thunderstorms Thursday to a Slight Risk for almost all 
of WV, with a Marginal Risk for the remainder of the area. With 
the high diurnally driven CAPE, and the afternoon timing of the
flat wave, probably also diurnally induced, the Strong to 
Severe Thunderstorm threat Thursday is strongly tied to diurnal
heating.

Isolated damaging wind gusts, localized flash flooding and hail
are all possible with stronger cores from mid afternoon into 
the early evening hours Thursday.

Broad long wave troughing sets up over the center of the 
continent during the latter portion of the work week, easing 
eastward to the central to eastern portion of the continent this
weekend. The ridging gives way to lead next mid/upper-level 
short wave trough as the long wave trough eases east Thursday 
night through Friday, pushing a surface cold front toward the 
area.

Adding synoptic-scale forcing and modest shear to the very 
moist and unstable air mass only solidifies the Severe 
Thunderstorm and Flash Flood threats for Friday afternoon and 
early evening, The Storm Prediction Center has a Slight Risk for
Severe Thunderstorms for the area Friday, while the Weather 
Prediction Center continues the Marginal Risk for Excessive 
Rainfall they has been carrying for the forecast area, in a 
long ribbon all along and ahead of the approaching cold front, 
for the Appalachians and Ohio Valley, and then back westward 
through the south-central Plains States.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

With mid/upper-level heights rebuilding in the wake of the 
short wave exiting today, above average temperatures return, to 
go along with the persistent high humidity of late, with lowland
highs in the upper 80s to low 90s Thursday and Friday, and 
lowland dew points and overnight lows in the upper 60s to mid 
70s through Friday.

A relative lull in shower and thunderstorm Thursday allows it 
to be the hottest day of the week. Lowland highs in the low 90s,
together with dew points in the low to mid 70s, will drive heat
indices to close to 100 degrees F for a time Thursday 
afternoon. This may eventually warrant Heat Advisories for 
portions of the lowlands for Thursday afternoon.
